The ABLATIVE is the by-word, the with-word
and the from-word of a Latin sentence.
Its commonest job names the means. No
word for 'with' is needed; the ending
= The soldiers were fortifying the camp
One ending, five jobs. Which is meant is

The first declension runs on -a, the

The second column is the one that counts.
Take off its -is and the stem is left.
Every other ending is built on that stem:
The card's cue, f., -is or m., -is, says
itself sits on the first Notes line.
One set of endings serves the whole family:
Subject and object match in the plural,
and neuters match in the singular too:
ōs and nōmen each do both jobs.
A smaller group, the i-stems, bends two
endings towards an i: ignium 'of the
fires', and often ignīs for the object.
urbs, ignis, arx and pars belong there.
Comparatives take these endings as well:
A preposition does not stand alone. It
fixes the case of the noun behind it, and
Those taking the ACCUSATIVE mark motion
ante oppidum   in front of the town
The ablative side follows. Its own five
jobs are set out in Lesson 18.
Those taking the ABLATIVE mark position,
the point left behind, or company:
ex oppidō      out of the town
ā takes a b before a vowel or an h:
in is the one to watch. It takes both
cases, and the case decides the sense:
in nāvēs impōnunt   they load onto
in castrīs manent   they stay inside
Read the pair, never the ending alone.
